Senses.Explanation: Literally, “guest-dust”: dust characterized as a visitor rather than the host. Much of the corpus preserves it in the inherited compound “guest-dust troubles” (客塵煩惱), something said to stain, cover, or be unrecognized. The distinct Chan deployment appears in Baizhang Huaihai's recorded classification: “one's own mind is buddha; illuminating function belongs to bodhisattva; mind after mind is the ruler; illuminating function belongs to guest-dust” (自心是佛，照用屬菩薩；心心是主宰，照用屬客塵). Here “guest-dust” is not merely a name for dirt or an outside visitor; Baizhang places it on the “illuminating function” side of a ruler/guest classification and immediately compares it to speaking of water by way of waves (如波說水). The Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings and the Expanded Lamp preserve this wording independently. Elsewhere the Records say a grown child learns explanations and does not know that these are “guest-dust troubles” (不知是客塵煩惱); Dahui speaks of the “stain of guest-dust troubles since beginningless time” (無始時來客塵煩惱之染); and the Admonitions for the Monastic Gate has the compact bodily compound “body-and-mind guest-dust” (身心客塵). The Zen record therefore keeps the inherited dust imagery but also bends it into Baizhang's explicit ruler/function classification.
Senses.Note: The corpus-wide sense remains one article because the Baizhang classification depends on the same guest-versus-ruler morphology as the broader compound. The explanation describes the recorded classification without adding an outside account of affliction or purity.

Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘probing pole and shadow grass.’ Linji's own record places the phrase third in his fourfold classification of a shout, after the Diamond King's jeweled sword and the crouching golden-haired lion and before a shout that does not function as a shout. Later records preserve it as a public category: masters are asked ‘what is a shout like probing pole and shadow grass?’ Recorded answers include ‘I have tested what bones you have’ (驗得你骨出) and ‘I know whether you are a dragon or a snake’ (知你是龍是蛇). A later comment calls a particular conversational move ‘also probing pole and shadow grass,’ and another record says a staff may function this way. These attested predicates place the ordinary images in encounters as a named testing gambit. The sources quoted here retain the compound and do not separately define the pole and the grass.
Senses.Note: 251 raw hits in 102 allowlist texts. Cross-checked all four Linji shout classifications. The simplified-graph variant (寻竿影草) was not adopted; the traditional probing-pole form (探竿影草) is the headword and dominant form. One corpus-wide sense is sufficient.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's record gives the complete fourfold classification, placing probing pole and shadow grass third.
